analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare drug plans to cover and steer patients toward cheaper generic and biosimilar versions.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to require Medicare drug plans to cover cheaper generics and biosimilars has sat untouched in the Senate Finance Committee since its April 2026 introduction, with no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill forces Medicare prescription drug plans to include cheaper generic drugs and biosimilars on their formularies whenever they cover the pricier brand-name original, and bars them from putting tougher hurdles like prior authorization on the cheaper copy than on the brand. It also requires a dedicated low-cost tier for generics and biosimilars, with copays at least $20 below the cheapest brand tier, and bans deductibles that apply only to generics. The new rules would start with plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2028.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who take drugs that have a cheaper generic or biosimilar available. They would be guaranteed access to the cheaper version at equal or lower cost-sharing, without extra gatekeeping hurdles, and their out-of-pocket costs would drop when plans steer them to the cheaper copy.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors on drugs with generics available

how_it_helps.text: Any Medicare plan whose formulary includes a brand-name reference drug must also include every cheaper approved generic of that drug, and at least one cheaper biosimilar for reference biologics where one is available.

Plans cannot impose access limits on the required generic or biosimilar — including prior authorization, utilization management, or step therapy — that are more restrictive than what the brand-name original faces, and cannot give the brand preferred status over the cheaper copy.
Plans with tiered cost-sharing must maintain a tier containing only generics and biosimilars, with either no cost-sharing or a copay at least $20 lower than the lowest brand-drug tier.

High-cost generics and biosimilars must get their own specialty tier with coinsurance at least 5 percentage points lower than any other specialty tier, and plans cannot approve a design with a deductible that applies only to generics or biosimilars.

analysis.who_pays: Part D insurers and Medicare Advantage plans lose flexibility in designing their drug formularies and cost-sharing, and may pass some of that cost into premiums. Brand-name drug makers and biologics manufacturers sell fewer brand units where a cheaper copy is guaranteed formulary placement and preferred cost-sharing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Part D insurers and brand-name drug makers

drawbacks.text: The requirements only take effect with plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2028, so beneficiaries see no relief before then.

Plans currently negotiate rebates from brand manufacturers that can subsidize premiums; because the bill requires generics and biosimilars to be preferred over the brand reference drugs, plans could lose some of that rebate leverage, and some added cost could surface in premiums.
The bill only affects formulary placement and cost-sharing for drugs that already have a cheaper approved copy; it does not cap prices for brand-name drugs with no generic or biosimilar competitor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors taking drugs with a cheaper generic or biosimilar available, the benefit is direct and concrete: guaranteed access to the cheaper version, no extra hoops, and lower copays. The main costs are borne by plan sponsors and brand manufacturers, and some could trickle into premiums through lost rebate leverage. The bill is narrow — it does nothing for brand-only drugs — but what it does, it does cleanly and mechanically.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or floor vote while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Senator James Lankford (R-OK) introduced the bill on April 16, 2026, joined by Senator Maggie Hassan (D-NH).
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action — no hearing, committee markup, or floor vote — has been recorded since the referral.
The bill has two cosponsors in total, both Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has not moved, Part D insurers and brand-name drug makers keep the current system, in which plans can exclude or deprioritize cheaper generics and biosimilars and steer patients toward higher-cost brand drugs. Medicare beneficiaries keep paying whatever their plan's formulary design delivers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Part D insurers and brand drug makers

for.name: Sen. James Lankford
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring Part D plans to cover and prefer cheaper generics and biosimilars.

for.name: Sen. Maggie Hassan
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its second sponsor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Mike Crapo (R-ID)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving it stalled since April 2026.

sides.party_line_note: The bill is bipartisan at its core — a Republican sponsor with two Democratic cosponsors — so its stall in committee has no recorded partisan vote against it; the record simply shows inaction after referral.

industries.note: Where a cheaper generic or biosimilar exists, plans must cover it, give it equal or better access than the brand, and put it on a tier at least $20 cheaper — displacing brand sales among Medicare enrollees. The industry's interest in keeping patients on higher-priced originals runs against beneficiaries' interest in paying less.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D insurers and Medicare Advantage plans
industries.note: Plans lose discretion to exclude or gatekeep cheaper generics and biosimilars and must restructure cost-sharing tiers, which could raise premiums through lost rebate leverage. They keep their role administering Part D either way.

The bill guarantees their products a place on every Medicare drug formulary and a cost-sharing tier at least $20 cheaper than the brand tier, increasing their sales. Their gain comes directly from beneficiaries paying less.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat untouched in the Senate Finance Committee since April 2026 with no hearing or markup and minimal cosponsorship (2). Most Senate bills die at this stage; the realistic path to passage would be attachment to a larger Medicare or health package, and standalone action this Congress is unlikely.
